body:
How information can influence social attitudes

Polarization occurs when opinions, attitudes or social identities become more sharply divided. It may appear as stronger disagreement about policies or as increasing distrust or hostility between groups. Social media can expose people to different viewpoints, but it can also repeatedly present material that confirms their existing beliefs.

Echo chambers and filter bubbles

An echo chamber is a communication environment in which people mainly encounter and reinforce similar views, often through their social connections and chosen information sources. Contradictory information may receive less attention or be dismissed.

A filter bubble refers to a pattern of limited information exposure associated particularly with personalised filtering or recommendations. The two concepts overlap, but they are not identical: an echo chamber emphasises social reinforcement, while a filter bubble emphasises the selection of information shown to a user.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to give greater attention or credibility to information that supports an existing belief. Emotional content, repetition, selective sharing and social approval can make misleading claims more persuasive.

Social media does not inevitably produce polarization. Research finds that effects vary across users, subjects, platform features and circumstances. Repeated exposure to similar material is not, by itself, proof that a person's opinions have become more extreme.

Fact-checking: testing the actual claim

Fact-checking is the examination of a verifiable claim against reliable evidence. It works best when the investigator identifies exactly what is being asserted instead of attempting to judge an entire post as one undivided statement.

A practical verification sequence

  1. Identify the claim. Determine whether the post asserts a date, quotation, number, event, policy decision or identity that can be checked.
  2. Find the original source. For an official order, look for the issuing department's original notification rather than a screenshot circulated by an unknown account.
  3. Check date and context. Establish whether a document is current, whether a photograph belongs to the claimed event and whether important qualifications have been omitted.
  4. Corroborate significant facts. Compare the claim with another suitable reliable source, especially when the issue is important or the first source is incomplete.
  5. Decide what the evidence supports. Treat confirmed, contradicted, misleading and still-unverified claims differently. Do not share a disputed claim as a fact simply because many accounts repeat it.

Checking photographs, videos and voices

An old image may be reused with a new caption. Searching for earlier appearances of the image can help establish whether it predates the alleged event. A short video may omit the question or surrounding statement that explains its meaning. In such cases, the complete original recording can be more useful than a forwarded excerpt.

For an alleged official audio message, compare the claim with the institution's authenticated communication channels. A voice resembling an official is not enough to prove that the person issued the message. Likewise, a platform label or automated detection result may be useful evidence but is not infallible.

Prevention, correction and responsible action

Media literacy helps citizens understand how information is produced, distributed and evaluated. Prebunking means explaining common misleading patterns before people encounter them. Debunking means correcting a particular false or misleading claim after it has appeared.

When a suspicious post arrives, citizens can avoid forwarding it, check the source and date, seek the original notice, and report impersonation or harmful content through the relevant platform or official channel. A citizen should avoid publicly accusing an individual of operating a foreign campaign or committing a crime without reliable evidence.

Fact-checking institutions

Independent fact-checking organisations, journalists and specialised verification teams may examine public claims. In India, the Press Information Bureau Fact Check Unit examines information relating to the policies, schemes and other business of the Government of India. Its scope is not the independent verification of every claim circulating in society. A government clarification may establish what the government officially announced; other questions may require additional evidence and scrutiny.

Prelims focus

  • Echo chambers involve reinforcement of similar views within an information environment.
  • Filter bubbles emphasise narrowed exposure through information selection or personalisation.
  • Confirmation bias favours information consistent with existing beliefs.
  • Prebunking occurs before exposure to a misleading claim; debunking addresses a claim after it appears.
  • PIB Fact Check focuses on information concerning the business of the Government of India.
  • Trap: A suspicious-looking video is not conclusively a deepfake, and repeated sharing is not proof of truth.

[NCERT, Social and Political Life II, Class 7, chapter 'Understanding Media', pp. 73–77, 2018–19 printing; OECD, Facts Not Fakes, 2024, sections on information integrity and societal resilience; UNESCO, Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms, 2023, media and information literacy; Press Information Bureau, 'About Factcheck', FAQs 13–15; UK House of Commons Library, 'How to verify images and videos', 2026; Nature, 'Misunderstanding the harms of online misinformation', 2024, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Checking the original record is more reliable than judging a viral post by appearance.

pictures.alt: Four ordered checks lead to evidence-based classification: supported, contradicted, misleading, or still unverified when evidence is insufficient.

title: Polarization, Fact-Checking and Protective Practices

body:
What is platform governance?

Platform governance refers to the rules, decisions and accountability mechanisms through which online services manage their information environment. It includes user agreements, content moderation, recommendation practices, complaint handling, transparency and compliance with law.

Content moderation means assessing or acting upon user-generated content under applicable rules. A platform may label material, limit its distribution, remove it or disable access to it. Content curation concerns how content is selected, organised and recommended to users. These functions are related but different: a post can remain available while its visibility changes.

Platform policies and legal requirements must also be distinguished. A platform may prohibit certain behaviour under its terms of service even when the behaviour does not independently amount to a criminal offence. Conversely, a legal order must follow the applicable statutory authority and procedure; it is not simply an ordinary moderation preference.

The Information Technology Rules, 2021

India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, framed under the Information Technology Act, 2000, impose due-diligence and grievance-related obligations on intermediaries. An intermediary generally provides a service that receives, stores or transmits electronic information on behalf of others. Social media intermediaries are a category of such services.

The Rules require covered intermediaries to publish relevant user policies and establish grievance arrangements. Significant social media intermediaries are those crossing the government-notified threshold of 50 lakh registered users in India and are subject to additional duties, including designated compliance and grievance personnel and periodic compliance reporting.

Complaints, appeals and legal notices

Under the Rules as amended through 10 February 2026, the ordinary grievance mechanism generally requires acknowledgement within 24 hours and resolution within 7 days. Specified removal complaints, including those concerning obscene content or impersonation, generally require resolution within 36 hours, subject to the separate 2-hour rule below. In particular, Rule 3(2)(b) provides a 2-hour period for taking reasonable and practicable removal or access-disabling measures in response to complaints about specified intimate or impersonation material.

Rule 3A provides for appeals to a Grievance Appellate Committee by a person dissatisfied with the grievance decision or whose grievance remains unresolved within the specified period. The prescribed appeal period is generally 30 days from communication of the grievance decision.

A separate rule concerns unlawful information covered by a valid court order or reasoned intimation from an appropriately authorised government officer. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in 2026, specifies removal or disabling of access within 3 hours after the prescribed form of actual knowledge. This is not a universal deadline for removing every disputed or allegedly false post.

The 2026 amendment concerning synthetic information

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026 on 10 February 2026. They came into force on 20 February 2026.

The amendment defines synthetically generated information in relation to realistically appearing artificially created or altered audio, visual or audiovisual information depicting an individual or event. The definition excludes specified routine or good-faith editing, technical improvements, accessibility measures and document-related work that do not materially misrepresent the underlying content.

Under Rule 3(3), covered intermediaries offering relevant synthetic-content functions must take reasonable and appropriate measures against unlawful synthetic content. Synthetic information not prohibited under that provision must be prominently labelled, with provenance information or appropriate mechanisms to the extent technically feasible. Rule 4(1A) additionally requires significant social media intermediaries that allow publication of information to obtain user declarations about synthetic content, take proportionate steps to verify those declarations and label identified synthetic content.

Synthetic does not mean illegal. The Rules distinguish unlawful synthetic content from other synthetic information that must be identified through the prescribed labelling arrangements.

Balancing safety and expression

Effective governance requires action against impersonation, unlawful content and privacy violations, but it also requires attention to errors, excessive restrictions and the rights of legitimate speakers. Clear reasons for decisions, opportunities to contest moderation and suitable human oversight can reduce unfair outcomes. International guidance similarly emphasises accountability, transparent moderation and freedom of expression.

Prelims focus

  • The IT Intermediary Rules were originally notified in 2021 under the IT Act, 2000.
  • The synthetic-information amendment was notified on 10 February 2026 and took effect on 20 February 2026.
  • Rule 3(3) addresses intermediary duties concerning synthetically generated information.
  • Rule 4(1A) creates additional declaration, verification and labelling duties for significant social media intermediaries.
  • Ordinary grievance resolution is generally within 7 days; specified intimate or impersonation complaints have a 2-hour action deadline.
  • Trap: The 3-hour period for prescribed legal notices is not the deadline for every user complaint.

[MeitY, Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, consolidated text updated 10 February 2026, rules 2, 3(1)(d), 3(2), 3(3), 3A, 4 and 4(1A); MeitY, Amendment Rules, 2026, G.S.R. 120(E), 10 February 2026, commencement provision; UNESCO, Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms, 2023, principles on transparency, accountability and freedom of expression; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: User complaints follow 24-hour, 7-day or specified 2-hour deadlines; valid legal directions require action within 3 hours after actual knowledge.
pictures.caption: A platform complaint and a valid legal direction follow different procedures.

title: Platform Governance and India's Rules on Synthetic Content

body:
Different institutions perform different security functions

India's cybersecurity arrangements include national incident-response institutions, specialised protection arrangements for critical infrastructure and sector-specific response teams. Their responsibilities overlap in coordination but differ in their principal purpose.

CERT-In: the national cyber incident-response agency

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) functions under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). Section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides the statutory basis for CERT-In as the national agency for performing specified cybersecurity functions.

Its work includes collecting and analysing information on cyber incidents, issuing alerts and advisories, coordinating incident-response activities and supporting measures to address cybersecurity incidents. A cyber incident may involve unauthorised access, disruption of digital services, a data leak or another event affecting computer security.

The 6-hour reporting requirement

On 28 April 2022, CERT-In issued directions under Section 70B(6). They require specified service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations to report the categories of cyber incidents covered by the directions within 6 hours of noticing the incident or having it brought to their notice.

The rule concerns covered entities and reportable incidents; it is not a general instruction that every citizen must report every suspicious social media message to CERT-In within 6 hours. Citizens reporting financial cyber fraud ordinarily use the designated cybercrime channels instead.

NCIIPC: protection of critical information infrastructure

The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) is the national nodal agency designated under Section 70A of the IT Act for critical information infrastructure protection. It functions under the administrative control of the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO).

Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) has a specific statutory meaning under Section 70: it is a computer resource whose incapacitation or destruction would have a debilitating impact on national security, the economy, public health or safety. Systems associated with electricity supply, financial services, transport or other essential services may be relevant to critical-infrastructure protection, depending on their actual importance and applicable designation.

NCIIPC's role includes coordination and advice directed at reducing risks to critical information infrastructure. It is not simply another name for CERT-In.

Sector-specific incident response

Some sectors have incident-response arrangements adapted to their operational needs. In the electricity sector, the Computer Security Incident Response Team – Power (CSIRT-Power) was constituted on 5 April 2023 as an extended arm of CERT-In and placed under the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). Its facility was inaugurated and became fully functional on 23 September 2024.

CSIRT-Power supports electricity-sector utilities through incident-related coordination, analysis, alerts and improved preparedness. The power sector also has specialised arrangements covering areas such as generation, transmission, distribution, grid operation and renewable energy.

For example, an incident affecting digital systems used by an electricity utility may involve the utility's own response arrangements and relevant sectoral coordination. CERT-In has the broader national incident-response role; NCIIPC has the specialised critical-information-infrastructure protection role when the affected systems meet the relevant criteria.

Incident response is not the same as criminal investigation

A cybersecurity incident may also be a crime, but technical incident coordination and criminal investigation are distinct functions. CERT-In and sectoral teams support cybersecurity response within their mandates. Police and other legally authorised investigating agencies handle criminal complaints and investigations under the applicable law.

Prelims focus

  • Section 70B: CERT-In, the national cyber incident-response agency under MeitY.
  • Section 70A: NCIIPC, the nodal agency for critical information infrastructure protection under NTRO.
  • Section 70: Definition of critical information infrastructure and provisions concerning protected systems.
  • CERT-In's directions dated 28 April 2022 prescribe 6-hour reporting for specified incidents by covered entities.
  • CSIRT-Power was constituted on 5 April 2023 under CEA and became fully functional on 23 September 2024.
  • Trap: CERT-In, NCIIPC and CSIRT-Power are not interchangeable institutions.

[Information Technology Act, 2000, sections 70, 70A and 70B; MeitY, Information Technology (National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) Rules, 2013, rules 3–4, notified 16 January 2014; CERT-In, Directions under Section 70B(6), 28 April 2022, paragraphs on functions and incident reporting, and related FAQs, May 2022; Central Electricity Authority, Annual Report 2024–25, section 5.19, 'Computer Security Incident Response Team – Power'; Ministry of Power, Lok Sabha reply on 'Cybersecurity of Power Grids', 2024; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
